context_blurb:
Your body is built of cells, the way a house is built of bricks. A cell is the smallest living unit, and most cells are far too tiny to see without a microscope. Plants, animals, mushrooms and bacteria are all made of cells, and everything a living thing does, from growing to healing, is cells at work.

In 1665, in his book Micrographia, Robert Hooke described a thin sliver of cork seen through his microscope. It was full of little box-shaped rooms, like the cells of a honeycomb, and he called them cells. Cork cells are dead, so their insides were long gone, and all Hooke could see of each one was the cell wall, holding air. A plant cell's stiff wall outlasts the living cell inside it.

Cell theory sums up what microscopes have shown since then in three big ideas. First, every living thing is made of one or more cells. A single bacterium is one whole living cell that does all the jobs of life by itself, while a person is built of around 30 trillion cells. A virus is not a cell at all, and molecules are the far smaller pieces that cells are built from. Second, the cell is the basic unit of life. Third, every new cell comes from a cell that already exists.

That third idea explains how a scraped knee heals. The scab is dried blood that shields the wound, and it never turns into skin. The new skin comes from living skin cells around and beneath the wound. Cells at its edges and deep in its floor split again and again. They creep across under the scab, which falls off once the new skin is done.

Cells come in two great kinds. Eukaryotes, which include amoebas as well as plant and animal cells, keep their genetic instructions, called DNA, inside a nucleus. Bacteria are prokaryotes, with no nucleus at all. A bacterium keeps its DNA in a loose clump in its cytoplasm, the jelly that fills the cell. Every cell is wrapped in a thin membrane. The membrane is the cell's gatekeeper: it controls what enters and leaves the cell, letting in water, oxygen and food and letting out wastes. In a plant or animal cell, the nucleus is the control centre. It holds the DNA and uses those instructions to direct the cell's work, such as making proteins. Mitochondria, found in plant and animal cells alike, release the energy stored in food.

A green leaf cell has extra parts. A leaf cell's chloroplasts make its food: they use the energy in sunlight, with water and carbon dioxide, to build sugar. Green chlorophyll inside them colours the leaf. Your cheek cells have none, so they cannot make food. Yet a leaf cell needs mitochondria too. Chloroplasts make the sugar, and mitochondria release the energy stored in that sugar so the cell can use it. A plant cell also has a stiff wall outside its membrane, for shape and support. One big central vacuole, a store of water, can fill most of a grown plant cell. When the central vacuole is full, it presses the cell out against its stiff wall, and that keeps the plant firm. Forget to water a potted plant and its vacuoles shrink, so it droops; water it and they swell and stand it up again. Animal cells have only small vacuoles, or none.

In a body of many cells, similar cells doing one job together form a tissue. Cardiac muscle, which squeezes with every heartbeat and makes up most of your heart, is a tissue of muscle cells. Two or more kinds of tissue make an organ, such as the heart itself. The heart, the blood vessels and the blood together make up an organ system, the circulatory system.
